claims.text: ProductsController.List() builds a ProductDto for each row as new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd), read from a Product entity queried via db.Products.

DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs defines ProductDto(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd), OrderItemDto(int ProductId, int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd), OrderDto(...), CreateOrderItemRequest(...), and CreateOrderRequest(List<CreateOrderItemRequest> Items) as records.
The Product entity in DonHang.Domain has exactly the properties Id, Name, and PriceVnd, the same three ProductDto lists.
The OrderItem entity in DonHang.Domain has OrderId, ProductId, Quantity, and UnitPriceVnd; OrderItemDto omits OrderId, keeping only ProductId, Quantity, and UnitPriceVnd.
The Customer entity in DonHang.Domain has a PasswordHash property alongside FullName, Email, and City.

ASP.NET Core's default JSON serialization for Web API controllers uses a camelCase naming policy, lowercasing the first letter of each C# property name for the JSON field name, unless configured otherwise.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs, Web API serialization defaults (System.Text.Json JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase)

claims.text: Sending GET /api/v1/products/1 to the running stage-1 lab returns 200 with body {"id":1,"name":"Bàn phím cơ","priceVnd":1250000} — camelCase field names, not PascalCase.

self_check.notes: Second lesson of rest-api on real stage-1 code (Dtos.cs was already tagged for this lesson during repo-stage). Used the real OrderItem/OrderItemDto field-omission (OrderId dropped) as a concrete 'only fields a client needs' example, and Customer.PasswordHash as a concrete 'why not just return the entity' cautionary example, instead of inventing a hypothetical.
